claim: SynGAP is a postsynaptic density (PSD) protein that binds to PDZ domains of the scaffold protein PSD-95.
source: SynGAP is a postsynaptic density (PSD) protein that binds to PDZ domains of the scaffold protein PSD-95.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Heterozygous deletion of Syngap1 in mice is correlated with increased steady-state levels of other key PSD proteins that bind PSD-95, although the level of PSD-95 remains constant.
source: We previously reported that heterozygous deletion of Syngap1 in mice is correlated with increased steady-state levels of other key PSD proteins that bind PSD-95, although the level of PSD-95 remains constant (Walkup et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The ratio to PSD-95 of Transmembrane AMPA-Receptor-associated Proteins (TARPs) was increased in young Syngap1+/- mice.
source: For example, the ratio to PSD-95 of Transmembrane AMPA-Receptor-associated Proteins (TARPs), which mediate binding of AMPA-type glutamate receptors to PSD-95, was increased in young Syngap1+/-mice.
evidence: This is stated as an example from previous work.

claim: Only females and not males show a highly significant correlation between an increase in TARP and a decrease in synGAP in the PSDs of Syngap1+/- rodents.
source: Here we show that only females and not males show a highly significant correlation between an increase in TARP and a decrease in synGAP in the PSDs of Syngap1+/-rodents.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by data presented in the results section.

claim: There is a sex difference in the adaptation of the PSD scaffold to synGAP haploinsufficiency.
source: The data reveal a sex difference in the adaptation of the PSD scaffold to synGAP haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is the conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: SynGAP is a Ras/Rap GTPase Activating Protein that is specifically expressed in neurons.
source: SynGAP is a Ras/Rap GTPase Activating Protein that is specifically expressed in neurons and is highly concentrated in the postsynaptic density (PSD) of glutamatergic synapses in the brain (Chen et al., 1998; Kim et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SynGAP is highly concentrated in the postsynaptic density (PSD) of glutamatergic synapses in the brain.
source: SynGAP is a Ras/Rap GTPase Activating Protein that is specifically expressed in neurons and is highly concentrated in the postsynaptic density (PSD) of glutamatergic synapses in the brain (Chen et al., 1998; Kim et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutations that cause heterozygous deletion or dysfunction of the human gene Syngap1 cause a severe form of intellectual disability (synGAP haploinsufficiency, also called Mental Retardation type 5 [MRD5]) often accompanied by autism and/or seizures.
source: Mutations that cause heterozygous deletion or dysfunction of the human gene Syngap1 cause a severe form of intellectual disability (synGAP haploinsufficiency, also called Mental Retardation type 5 [MRD5]) often accompanied by autism and/or seizures (Berryer et al., 2013; Hamdan et al., 2011; Hamdan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In mice, heterozygous deletion of the gene Syngap1 causes similar neurological deficits to those seen in humans.
source: In mice, heterozygous deletion of the gene Syngap1 causes similar neurological deficits; homozygous deletion causes death a few days after birth (Komiyama et al., 2002; Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Homozygous deletion of Syngap1 in mice causes death a few days after birth.
source: In mice, heterozygous deletion of the gene Syngap1 causes similar neurological deficits; homozygous deletion causes death a few days after birth (Komiyama et al., 2002; Vazquez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: One function of synGAP is to regulate the balance of active Ras and Rap at the postsynaptic membrane.
source: One function of synGAP is to regulate the balance of active Ras and Rap at the postsynaptic membrane (Walkup et al., 2015), thereby controlling the balance of exocytosis and endocytosis of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (Zhu et al., 2002) and contributing to regulation of the actin cytoskeleton (Tolias et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SynGAP controls the balance of exocytosis and endocytosis of AMPA-type glutamate receptors.
source: One function of synGAP is to regulate the balance of active Ras and Rap at the postsynaptic membrane (Walkup et al., 2015), thereby controlling the balance of exocytosis and endocytosis of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (Zhu et al., 2002) and contributing to regulation of the actin cytoskeleton (Tolias et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SynGAP contributes to regulation of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: One function of synGAP is to regulate the balance of active Ras and Rap at the postsynaptic membrane (Walkup et al., 2015), thereby controlling the balance of exocytosis and endocytosis of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (Zhu et al., 2002) and contributing to regulation of the actin cytoskeleton (Tolias et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: SynGAP helps to regulate anchoring of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) in the PSD.
source: In a recent paper in eLife (Walkup et al., 2016), we postulated that synGAP also helps to regulate anchoring of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) in the PSD.
evidence: This is a hypothesis postulated in previous work by the authors.

claim: AMPARs are tethered to the scaffold protein PSD-95 by auxiliary subunits called TARPs.
source: AMPARs are tethered to the scaffold protein PSD-95 by auxiliary subunits called TARPs (Transmembrane AMPA Receptor-associated Proteins, Tomita et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TARPs contain a PDZ ligand that binds to PDZ domains in PSD-95.
source: TARPs contain a PDZ ligand that binds to PDZ domains in PSD-95.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: An early event in induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) is increased trapping of AMPARs that is mediated by enhanced binding of TARPs to PDZ domains.
source: An early event in induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) is increased trapping of AMPARs that is mediated by enhanced binding of TARPs to PDZ domains (Opazo and Choquet, 2011; Tomita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SynGAP is anchored in the PSD by binding of its α1 splice variant to the PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: SynGAP is also anchored in the PSD by binding of its α1 splice variant to the PDZ domains of PSD-95 (Kim et al., 1998; McMahon et al., 2012; Walkup et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SynGAP is nearly as abundant in the PSD fraction as PSD-95.
source: SynGAP is nearly as abundant in the PSD fraction as PSD-95, which suggests that it occupies a large fraction of the PDZ domains and can compete with TARPs for binding to PSD-95 (Chen et al., 1998; Dosemeci et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SynGAP occupies a large fraction of the PDZ domains and can compete with TARPs for binding to PSD-95.
source: SynGAP is nearly as abundant in the PSD fraction as PSD-95, which suggests that it occupies a large fraction of the PDZ domains and can compete with TARPs for binding to PSD-95 (Chen et al., 1998; Dosemeci et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the abundance of synGAP and supported by citations.

claim: During induction of LTP, calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) phosphorylates synGAP, increasing the rate of inactivation of Rap relative to Ras.
source: During induction of LTP, calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) phosphorylates synGAP, increasing the rate of inactivation of Rap relative to Ras, and, at the same time, causing a decrease in the affinity of synGAP-α1 for the PDZ domains of PSD-95 (Walkup et al., 2015; Walkup et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: CaMKII phosphorylation of synGAP causes a decrease in the affinity of synGAP-α1 for the PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: During induction of LTP, calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) phosphorylates synGAP, increasing the rate of inactivation of Rap relative to Ras, and, at the same time, causing a decrease in the affinity of synGAP-α1 for the PDZ domains of PSD-95 (Walkup et al., 2015; Walkup et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The decreased affinity of synGAP for PSD-95 might contribute to induction of LTP by allowing TARPs and their associated AMPARs to compete more effectively for binding to the PDZ domains.
source: We postulated that the decreased affinity of synGAP for PSD-95 might contribute to induction of LTP by allowing TARPs and their associated AMPARs to compete more effectively for binding to the PDZ domains and thus increase their anchoring in the PSD.
evidence: This is a hypothesis postulated by the authors.

claim: Induction of LTP would be disrupted in synGAP heterozygotes because the transient shift in competition for PDZ binding by synGAP would be less potent because of loss of a copy of Syngap1.
source: If this hypothesis is correct, one consequence could be that induction of LTP would be disrupted in synGAP heterozygotes because the transient shift in competition for PDZ binding by synGAP would be less potent because of loss of a copy of Syngap1.
evidence: This is a speculative consequence of the hypothesis.

claim: The steady state level of TARPs bound to PSD-95 in PSDs would be increased in synGAP heterozygotes because the steady state level of synGAP is reduced.
source: A second possible consequence could be that the steady state level of TARPs bound to PSD-95 in PSDs would be increased in synGAP heterozygotes because the steady state level of synGAP is reduced.
evidence: This is a speculative consequence of the hypothesis.

claim: In the Walkup et al. 2016 study, the mean ratio of synGAP to PSD-95 was 25% less in PSDs from HET mice compared to WT.
source: The mean ratio of synGAP to PSD-95 was 25% less in PSDs from the HET mice compared to WT.
evidence: This is a result from the previous study cited.

claim: In the Walkup et al. 2016 study, the mean ratio of TARPs to PSD-95 showed a small (12%) but significant increase in PSDs from the HET animals compared to WT.
source: As we had predicted, the mean ratio of TARPs to PSD-95 showed a small (12%) but significant increase in PSDs from the HET animals compared to WT.
evidence: This is a result from the previous study cited.

claim: In the Walkup et al. 2016 study, there was a small but significant increase in the mean ratio of LRRTM2 (14%) and neuroligin-2 (9%) to PSD-95.
source: We also found a small but significant increase in the mean ratio of LRRTM2 (14%) and neuroligin-2 (9%) to PSD-95.
evidence: This is a result from the previous study cited.

claim: In the Walkup et al. 2016 study, the mean ratio of neuroligin-1 to PSD-95 was unchanged.
source: The mean ratio of neuroligin-1 to PSD-95 was unchanged.
evidence: This is a result from the previous study cited.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 technology was used to establish a Syngap1 KO rat line that harbors a frameshift mutation in exon8 of Syngap1.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 technology was used to establish a Syngap1 KO rat line that harbors a frameshift mutation in exon8 of Syngap1 (Figure 1A), which prevents expression of the protein.
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by Figure 1A.

claim: The frameshift mutation in exon8 of Syngap1 prevents expression of the protein.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 technology was used to establish a Syngap1 KO rat line that harbors a frameshift mutation in exon8 of Syngap1 (Figure 1A), which prevents expression of the protein.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the mutation.

claim: SynGAP protein expression level is reduced by 50% in HET knockout rats compared to wild-type.
source: SynGAP protein expression level is reduced by 50% in HET knockout rats compared to wild-type (WT) and is absent in homozygous knockouts (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SynGAP protein is absent in homozygous knockout rats.
source: SynGAP protein expression level is reduced by 50% in HET knockout rats compared to wild-type (WT) and is absent in homozygous knockouts (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SynGAP KO rats die perinatally.
source: While SynGAP KO rats die perinatally, SynGAP HET rats appear healthy and fertile.
evidence: This is an observation from the rat model.

claim: SynGAP HET rats appear healthy and fertile.
source: While SynGAP KO rats die perinatally, SynGAP HET rats appear healthy and fertile.
evidence: This is an observation from the rat model.

claim: PSD fractions were prepared from the forebrains of 165 individual rodents, comprising 82 WT and 83 HETs.
source: PSD fractions were prepared from the forebrains of 165 individual rodents, comprising 82 WT and 83 HETs.
evidence: This describes the sample size of the study.

claim: The total sample included 81 females (39 WT, 42 HET), and 84 males (43 WT, 41 HET).
source: The total sample included 81 females (39 WT, 42 HET), and 84 males (43 WT, 41 HET).
evidence: This describes the sample composition by sex and genotype.

claim: Approximately half of the animals were rats and half were mice; approximately half were 7.5 weeks old and half were 12.5 weeks old.
source: In each category, approximately half of the animals were rats and half were mice; approximately half were 7.5 weeks old and half were 12.5 weeks old.
evidence: This describes the sample composition by species and age.

claim: The synGAP/PSD-95 ratio is reduced by 22% in HET rodents compared to WT.
source: As expected, the synGAP/PSD-95 ratio (Figure 2A, left) is reduced by 22% in HET rodents compared to WT (the WT level is indicated by a dotted line).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ratio of TARP to PSD-95 is not significantly different between WT and HET rodents when averaged over all animals.
source: However, the ratio of TARP to PSD-95 (Figure 2B, left) is not significantly different, even when the results were averaged for animals grouped by sex, species, and age (Figure 2A and B), except for seven wk old female mice in which the ratio of TARPs to PSD-95 was significantly reduced compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In seven week old female mice, the ratio of TARPs to PSD-95 was significantly reduced compared to WT.
source: However, the ratio of TARP to PSD-95 (Figure 2B, left) is not significantly different, even when the results were averaged for animals grouped by sex, species, and age (Figure 2A and B), except for seven wk old female mice in which the ratio of TARPs to PSD-95 was significantly reduced compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The reduced TARP/PSD-95 ratio in 7 week old female mice may have been influenced by a developmental effect causing lower overall expression of TARPs in 7 week old mice.
source: This value may have been influenced by a developmental effect causing lower overall expression of TARPs in 7 week old mice.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: There is more variability in the averaged ratios of TARP to PSD-95 for females compared to males.
source: We also noted more variability in the averaged ratios of TARP to PSD-95 for females (Figure 2B, right) compared to males (Figure 2B, middle).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At steady state in vivo, lower amounts of synGAP in PSDs from HET animals correlate with higher amounts of TARP.
source: These data show that, at steady state in vivo, lower amounts of synGAP in PSDs from the HET animals (Figure 3C) correlate with higher amounts of TARP; whereas there is no correlation in WT animals (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: There is no correlation between synGAP and TARP levels in WT animals.
source: These data show that, at steady state in vivo, lower amounts of synGAP in PSDs from the HET animals (Figure 3C) correlate with higher amounts of TARP; whereas there is no correlation in WT animals (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The data from all females show an inverse correlation between synGAP/PSD-95 and TARP/PSD-95 ratios that just reaches statistical significance.
source: The data from all females (Figure 3D) show an inverse correlation between the two ratios that just reaches statistical significance.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The data from all males shows no correlation between synGAP/PSD-95 and TARP/PSD-95 ratios.
source: In contrast, the data from all males (Figure 3G) shows no correlation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: WT females and WT males show no correlation between synGAP/PSD-95 and TARP/PSD-95 ratios.
source: Similarly, WT females and WT males (Figure 3E and H) show no correlation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and 3H.

claim: The data from HET females show the largest inverse correlation of all the data sets, with a Spearman's r = −0.498 and a p-value=0.0006.
source: Strikingly, the data from HET females (Figure 3F) show the largest inverse correlation of all the data sets, with a Spearman's r = −0.498 and a p-value=0.0006.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: HET males show no significant correlation between synGAP/PSD-95 and TARP/PSD-95 ratios.
source: HET males (Figure 3I) show no significant correlation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The strong inverse correlation between the amount of synGAP and the amount of TARP in PSDs from HET females likely drives the inverse correlation observed for pooled HET animals and pooled females.
source: The strong inverse correlation between the amount of synGAP and the amount of TARP in PSDs from HET females (Figure 3F) likely drives the inverse correlation observed for pooled HET animals (Figure 3C) and pooled females (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data patterns observed.

claim: The amounts of PSD-95 per PSD protein are not statistically different between HETs and WT or between male and female subgroups.
source: We established that the amounts of PSD-95 per PSD protein are not statistically different between HETs and WT or between male and female subgroups; they are also not correlated with synGAP levels among individuals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PSD-95 levels are not correlated with synGAP levels among individuals.
source: We established that the amounts of PSD-95 per PSD protein are not statistically different between HETs and WT or between male and female subgroups; they are also not correlated with synGAP levels among individuals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences among individuals in the target protein/PSD-95 ratio can be interpreted as actual differences in the concentrations of the target protein in the PSD fractions.
source: Thus, differences among individuals in the target protein/PSD-95 ratio can be interpreted as actual differences in the concentrations of the target protein in the PSD fractions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that PSD-95 levels are constant.

claim: Between 7.5 and 12.5 weeks of age, synGAP haploinsufficiency has a much greater effect on the content of TARPs in the PSDs of female animals than in those of males.
source: These results mean that, between 7.5 and 12.5 weeks of age, synGAP haploinsufficiency has a much greater effect on the content of TARPs in the PSDs of female animals than in those of males.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: In HET females, the structure of the PSD is such that TARP and synGAP compete directly for binding to PSD-95.
source: The simplest explanation is that in HET females, the structure of the PSD, which is determined by multiple equilibria among several proteins, is such that TARP and synGAP compete directly for binding to PSD-95; whereas in HET males, this particular competition is not significant.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: In HET males, competition between TARP and synGAP for binding to PSD-95 is not significant.
source: The simplest explanation is that in HET females, the structure of the PSD, which is determined by multiple equilibria among several proteins, is such that TARP and synGAP compete directly for binding to PSD-95; whereas in HET males, this particular competition is not significant.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: There is a statistically significant inverse correlation between TARP/PSD-95 and synGAP/PSD-95 in HET female mice at both 7.5 and 12.5 weeks.
source: Nevertheless, they show a statistically significant inverse correlation between TARP/PSD-95 and synGAP/PSD-95 in HET female mice at both 7.5 and 12.5 weeks.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In data from HET rats at 7.5 weeks, the inverse correlation between TARP/PSD-95 and synGAP/PSD-95 is very close to significance.
source: In data from HET rats at 7.5 weeks, the inverse correlation is very close to significance; at 12.5 weeks, it is less significant, but still shows a trend.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In HET rats at 12.5 weeks, the inverse correlation between TARP/PSD-95 and synGAP/PSD-95 is less significant, but still shows a trend.
source: In data from HET rats at 7.5 weeks, the inverse correlation is very close to significance; at 12.5 weeks, it is less significant, but still shows a trend.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the corresponding males, none of the data sets shows a statistically significant inverse correlation between TARP/PSD-95 and synGAP/PSD-95.
source: In the corresponding males, none of the data sets shows a statistically significant inverse correlation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Competition between synGAP and TARP for binding to PSD-95 in females is more prominent at 7 weeks than at 12 weeks.
source: More data would be required to make a definitive conclusion, but the results suggest that competition between synGAP and TARP for binding to PSD-95 in females is more prominent at 7 weeks than at 12 weeks, and more prominent in mice than in rats.
evidence: This is a tentative conclusion based on the data trends.

claim: Competition between synGAP and TARP for binding to PSD-95 in females is more prominent in mice than in rats.
source: More data would be required to make a definitive conclusion, but the results suggest that competition between synGAP and TARP for binding to PSD-95 in females is more prominent at 7 weeks than at 12 weeks, and more prominent in mice than in rats.
evidence: This is a tentative conclusion based on the data trends.

claim: GluN2B exhibits a highly significant reduction of about 10% in HETs compared to WT.
source: GluN2B exhibits a highly significant reduction of about 10% in HETs compared to WT; NLG-1 shows no change; and NLG-2 increases significantly by about 7%.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NLG-1 shows no change in HETs compared to WT.
source: GluN2B exhibits a highly significant reduction of about 10% in HETs compared to WT; NLG-1 shows no change; and NLG-2 increases significantly by about 7%.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: NLG-2 increases significantly by about 7% in HETs compared to WT.
source: GluN2B exhibits a highly significant reduction of about 10% in HETs compared to WT; NLG-1 shows no change; and NLG-2 increases significantly by about 7%.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is no significant difference in the ratios of GluN2B, NLG-1, and NLG-2 to PSD-95 between rat and mouse, males and females, or between 7.5 week and 12.5 week old animals.
source: There is no significant difference in these ratios between rat and mouse, males and females, or between 7.5 week and 12.5 week old animals.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the data in Figure 4.

claim: The absence of any change in NLG-1 and the slight increase in NLG-2 recapitulate findings in Walkup et al. (2016).
source: The absence of any change in NLG-1 and the slight increase in NLG-2 recapitulate our findings in Walkup et al. (2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work by the authors.

claim: The concentration of GluN2B in PSDs shows a strong positive correlation with the amount of synGAP (rank correlation coefficient ≈ 0.4).
source: In contrast to TARPs, the concentration of GluN2B in PSDs shows a strong positive correlation with the amount of synGAP (rank correlation coefficient ≈ 0.4), and is reduced in Syngap1 HETs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: GluN2B concentration is reduced in Syngap1 HETs.
source: In contrast to TARPs, the concentration of GluN2B in PSDs shows a strong positive correlation with the amount of synGAP (rank correlation coefficient ≈ 0.4), and is reduced in Syngap1 HETs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The rank correlation between GluN2B and synGAP is significant in both WT and HET animals and does not differ between males and females.
source: The rank correlation among individual animals is significant in both WT and HET animals and does not differ between males and females (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: SynGAP plays a role in localizing GluN2B to the PSD, but it is not the only protein involved.
source: This data shows that synGAP plays a role in localizing GluN2B to the PSD, but that it is not the only protein involved.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: The amount of synGAP in the PSD does not influence the amount of NLG-1.
source: We reproduced our original finding that the amount of synGAP in the PSD does not influence the amount of NLG-1 and shows a trend toward a small inverse correlation with the amount of NLG-2 in PSDs (Walkup et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and reproduces previous findings.

claim: The amount of synGAP shows a trend toward a small inverse correlation with the amount of NLG-2 in PSDs.
source: We reproduced our original finding that the amount of synGAP in the PSD does not influence the amount of NLG-1 and shows a trend toward a small inverse correlation with the amount of NLG-2 in PSDs (Walkup et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and reproduces previous findings.

claim: Although both synGAP and NLG-1 bind to PDZ3 of PSD-95, reduction of synGAP does not increase the steady-state amount of NLG-1 in the PSD in vivo.
source: Thus, although both synGAP and NLG-1 (Irie et al., 1997) bind to PDZ3 of PSD-95, reduction of synGAP does not increase the steady-state amount of NLG-1 in the PSD in vivo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data combined with cited knowledge.

claim: NLG's have a higher affinity for PDZ3 than synGAP such that synGAP does not compete effectively with them for binding to PDZ3 in vivo.
source: The simplest explanation is that NLG's have a higher affinity for PDZ3 than synGAP such that synGAP does not compete effectively with them for binding to PDZ3 in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: A protein fragment containing all three PDZ domains of PSD-95 was found to have a KD of ~200 nM for a 16mer with the sequence of the carboxyl terminus of NLG-1.
source: A protein fragment containing all three PDZ domains of PSD-95 was found to have a KD of ~200 nM for a 16mer with the sequence of the carboxyl terminus of NLG-1 (Irie et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Nearly full length synGAP, missing only the first 100 residues of the amino-terminus, has an affinity for PDZ3 of ~650 nM and for a fragment containing all three PDZ domains of 5 nM.
source: In our recent study, we found that nearly full length synGAP, missing only the first 100 residues of the amino-terminus, has an affinity for PDZ3 of ~650 nM and for a fragment containing all three PDZ domains of 5 nM.
evidence: This is a result from the authors' recent study.

claim: The competition for binding to PDZ3 between NLG's and synGAP is likely influenced by additional binding sites on PSD-95 or on other scaffold proteins for NLG's and/or synGAP.
source: It is likely that the competition for binding to PDZ3 between NLG's and synGAP is influenced by additional binding sites on PSD-95 or on other scaffold proteins for NLG's and/or synGAP.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the complexity of the interactions.

claim: SynGAP can compete with some proteins for localization in the PSD and it can help to concentrate others.
source: These results illustrate the complex role that synGAP plays in modulating the steady-state composition of the PSD. It can compete with some proteins for localization in the PSD and it can help to concentrate others.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the results.

claim: The structure of the PSD is a dynamic equilibrium governed by multiple protein associations and driven by the relative concentrations of each protein and the affinities of their mutual binding domains.
source: The results are consistent with the concept that the structure of the PSD is a dynamic equilibrium governed by multiple protein associations and driven by the relative concentrations of each protein and the affinities of their mutual binding domains.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation consistent with the data.

claim: Phosphorylation of synGAP by CaMKII reduces the affinity of synGAP for all three of the PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: Our earlier finding that phosphorylation of synGAP by CaMKII, which is activated upon induction of LTP, reduces the affinity of synGAP for all three of the PDZ domains of PSD-95 suggests that post-translational modulation of synGAP's affinity for PSD-95 may initiate transient reorganization of the PSD in stimulated synapses.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' earlier work.

claim: Post-translational modulation of synGAP's affinity for PSD-95 may initiate transient reorganization of the PSD in stimulated synapses.
source: Our earlier finding that phosphorylation of synGAP by CaMKII, which is activated upon induction of LTP, reduces the affinity of synGAP for all three of the PDZ domains of PSD-95 suggests that post-translational modulation of synGAP's affinity for PSD-95 may initiate transient reorganization of the PSD in stimulated synapses.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on earlier findings.

claim: Disruption of the transient role of synGAP likely contributes to the phenotypes of synGAP haploinsufficiency, but in ways that may not differ between females and males.
source: Disruption of this transient role likely contributes to the phenotypes of synGAP haploinsufficiency, but in ways that may not differ between females and males.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: The most striking new result of this research advance is the discovery of a sex difference in the adaptation of the PSD scaffold to synGAP haploinsufficiency.
source: The most striking new result of this research advance is the discovery of a sex difference in the adaptation of the PSD scaffold to synGAP haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: A decrease in the steady-state concentration of synGAP in rodent PSDs correlates with a higher concentration of TARPs in PSDs only in females and not in males.
source: Specifically, we show that a decrease in the steady-state concentration of synGAP in rodent PSDs correlates with a higher concentration of TARPs in PSDs only in females and not in males.
evidence: This is the main finding summarized in the Discussion.

claim: In female HETs, the rank correlation coefficient between the concentrations of TARP and synGAP in PSDs is −0.5.
source: In female HETs, the rank correlation coefficient between the concentrations of TARP and synGAP in PSDs is −0.5, which suggests a relatively high competition between the two proteins for binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95 in vivo.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The rank correlation coefficient of −0.5 suggests a relatively high competition between TARP and synGAP for binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95 in vivo in female HETs.
source: In female HETs, the rank correlation coefficient between the concentrations of TARP and synGAP in PSDs is −0.5, which suggests a relatively high competition between the two proteins for binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95 in vivo.

claim: Competition between TARP and synGAP does not affect the composition of PSDs in male HETs.
source: This competition does not affect the composition of PSDs in male HETs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of correlation in males.

claim: SynGAP haploinsufficiency causes about 4% of cases of sporadic intellectual disability (ID) in humans, often accompanied by seizures and autistic behaviors.
source: SynGAP haploinsufficiency causes about 4% of cases of sporadic intellectual disability (ID) in humans, often accompanied by seizures and autistic behaviors (Berryer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: If the sex difference in the interaction of synGAP with TARPs in the rodent PSD is also present in humans, it might result in differences between girls and boys in the prevalence of some of the associated symptoms.
source: If the sex difference in the interaction of synGAP with TARPs in the rodent PSD is also present in humans, it might result in differences between girls and boys in the prevalence of some of the associated symptoms.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications for humans.

claim: The PSD is formed by multiple interactions among the major scaffold proteins and 'client' signaling proteins which are concentrated in the PSD by their association with the scaffold proteins.
source: The PSD is formed by multiple interactions among the major scaffold proteins and 'client' signaling proteins which are concentrated in the PSD by their association with the scaffold proteins (Kennedy, 2016; Kennedy et al., 2005; Sheng and Kim, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At any one time, the composition of a PSD is a dynamic equilibrium among all the possible protein associations, driven by the relative concentrations of each protein in a spine, and the relative affinities of their mutual binding domains.
source: At any one time, the composition of a PSD is a dynamic equilibrium among all the possible protein associations, driven by the relative concentrations of each protein in a spine, and the relative affinities of their mutual binding domains (e.g. Gray et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There is a difference between males and females in the composition or regulation of proteins in PSDs which causes the concentration of TARPs in PSDs to be sensitive to the steady-state concentration of synGAP in females, but not males.
source: The simplest interpretation of our present result isthat there is a difference between males and females in the composition or regulation of proteins in PSDs which causes the concentration of TARPs in PSDs to be sensitive to the steady-state concentration of synGAP in females, but not males.

claim: There is no difference between males and females in the amount of synGAP in PSDs of either genotype.

evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: TARPs have been shown to immobilize AMPARs at the synaptic site by binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95.
source: TARPs are subunits of AMPARs, and have been shown to immobilize AMPARs at the synaptic site by binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95 (Opazo and Choquet, 2011; Tomita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SynGAP-α1 competes with TARPs for binding to PSD-95 and therefore helps to limit the number of AMPARs immobilized at the synapse.
source: In our recent eLife paper, we postulated that synGAP-α1, which contains a PDZ ligand, competes with TARPs for binding to PSD-95 and therefore helps to limit the number of AMPARs immobilized at the synapse (Walkup et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis postulated in previous work by the authors.

claim: Transient phosphorylation of synGAP by CaMKII during induction of LTP will allow more binding of TARP to the PDZ domains and thus contribute to increased trapping of AMPARs.
source: One is that transient phosphorylation of synGAP by CaMKII during induction of LTP, which reduces the affinity of its PDZ ligand for PSD-95, will allow more binding of TARP to the PDZ domains; and thus contribute to increased trapping of AMPARs.
evidence: This is a speculative corollary of the hypothesis.

claim: In HET rodents, which have a reduced concentration of synGAP, the concentration of TARPs (and thus AMPARs) in the PSD will be higher than in WT if the concentration of synGAP in WTs is high enough to effectively compete with binding of TARPs to PSD-95.
source: If, at steady-state, the concentration of synGAP in WTs is high enough to effectively compete with binding of TARPs to PSD-95, then, in HET rodents, which have a reduced concentration of synGAP, the concentration of TARPs (and thus AMPARs) in the PSD will be higher than in WT.
evidence: This is a speculative corollary of the hypothesis.

claim: The analysis supports the hypothesis that synGAP-α1 does indeed compete with steady-state binding of TARPs to PSD-95 in some circumstances.
source: The analysis supports the hypothesis that synGAP-α1 does indeed compete with steady-state binding of TARPs to PSD-95 in some circumstances.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data analysis.

claim: One possible mechanistic explanation for the sex difference is that additional protein(s) are present in females that compete with synGAP for binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95, resulting in 'crowding' that makes binding of TARP to PSD-95 more sensitive to reduction of synGAP in females.
source: One simple one is that additional protein(s) are present in females that compete with synGAP for binding to PDZ domains of PSD-95. The resulting 'crowding' could make binding of TARP to PSD-95 more sensitive to reduction of synGAP in females.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation.

claim: Another possible mechanistic explanation is that an additional protein which can compete with TARPs more strongly than synGAP for binding to PSD-95 is present in male PSDs, but not in female PSDs.
source: Another is that an additional protein which can compete with TARPs more strongly than synGAP for binding to PSD-95 is present in male PSDs, but not in female PSDs. In this case, reduction of synGAP in PSDs of males would be expected to have little effect on the concentration of TARPs.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation.

claim: Despite any differences between males and females in mechanism, the mean steady-state ratio of TARPs to PSD-95 in the two sexes is not significantly different among WTs or HETs.
source: Interestingly, despite any differences between males and females in mechanism, the mean steady-state ratio of TARPs to PSD-95 in the two sexes is not significantly different among WTs or HETs.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: 7 to 12 week old female rodents have higher synaptic levels of membrane estrogen receptor alpha (mERalpha) than males.
source: Wang et al. (2018) found that 7 to 12 week old female rodents (the same age range used in our study) have higher synaptic levels of membrane estrogen receptor alpha (mERalpha) and, in contrast to males, require activation of mERalpha for activation of some of the signaling kinases that support long-term potentiation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In 7 to 12 week old female rodents, activation of mERalpha is required for activation of some of the signaling kinases that support long-term potentiation, in contrast to males.
source: Wang et al. (2018) found that 7 to 12 week old female rodents (the same age range used in our study) have higher synaptic levels of membrane estrogen receptor alpha (mERalpha) and, in contrast to males, require activation of mERalpha for activation of some of the signaling kinases that support long-term potentiation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.
